blockMcqs.question: Which SQL object stores query results on disk?
options: A regular view
A synonym
A materialized view
An index
blockMcqs.explanation: A regular view stores only the query definition; a materialized view stores the actual result rows on disk.

blockMcqs.question: What does querying a view actually do?
options: Reads pre-stored rows from the view
Re-executes the saved SELECT on the base tables
Copies data into a temp table first
Reads from an index instead of the table
blockMcqs.explanation: A view stores only the query definition. Each SELECT re-runs it against the live underlying tables.

blockMcqs.question: Which condition makes a view read-only?
options: The view has a WHERE clause
The view uses ORDER BY
The view includes a JOIN or GROUP BY
The view selects only one column
blockMcqs.explanation: Views with JOINs, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, or aggregates cannot be updated — the DB can't map a write back to one base row.

blockMcqs.question: What is the main trade-off of a materialized view?
options: Cannot use SQL to query it
Stored result can become stale
Slower to read than a regular view
Only works with one base table
blockMcqs.explanation: The snapshot is only as fresh as the last REFRESH — base table changes are not reflected until then.

blockMcqs.question: When should you prefer a regular view over a materialized view?
options: When the query is slow and data can be slightly stale
When you always need live, up-to-date results
When you want to avoid writing SQL
When disk space is unlimited
blockMcqs.explanation: Regular views re-run the query on every access, so they always return current data — the right choice when freshness matters.

blockMcqs.question: What is a full table scan?
options: Reading every row in a table to find matches
Scanning only the index without touching rows
Copying the table to a temp buffer
Refreshing statistics on the table
blockMcqs.explanation: Without an index, the DB reads every row to find the ones matching the query — called a full table scan, expensive on large tables.

blockMcqs.question: Why do sequences produce gaps even without data loss?
options: Concurrent users share one counter
Rolled-back transactions still consume sequence values
The DB rounds values to avoid conflicts
Sequences skip even numbers by default
blockMcqs.explanation: NEXTVAL advances the sequence before the transaction commits. If the transaction rolls back, the value is gone — gaps are expected and normal.

blockMcqs.question: What is the main benefit of a synonym?
options: Speeds up queries by caching results
Lets you rename a column permanently
Provides an alias so one name hides the real object location
Enforces access control on tables
blockMcqs.explanation: A synonym is a stable alias. When the underlying object moves or is renamed, you update the synonym once instead of every query.
